title: The Science of Fear Why We Love to Be Scared
paragraphs: Every year, millions of people watch horror movies and visit haunted houses, even though they know they will be frightened. Why do so many people enjoy being scared? Scientists have been studying this question.

According to Margee Kerr, a sociologist at the University of Pittsburgh, fear activates the body's nervous system. When there is no real danger, this feeling can be experienced as excitement. In addition, getting through a scary experience can give people a sense of achievement. In one study, Kerr and her colleagues surveyed about 260 adults after they visited a haunted house. About half of them were in a better mood afterward, especially those who felt they had faced their fears.

Not everyone enjoys horror for the same reasons. Researchers Mathias Clasen and Coltan Scrivner surveyed about 250 American horror fans and found three types. "Adrenaline junkies" love the rush and say that being scared makes them feel alive. "White knucklers" feel more stressed and sometimes have nightmares, but they still watch horror. Finally, "dark copers" use horror to help them deal with difficult feelings in their own lives. In another study, Clasen's team found that horror fans were slightly more likely to be thrill-seekers.

Some research suggests horror may even be useful. According to Scrivner, horror allows people to practice dealing with feelings of fear. In a survey of more than 300 Americans in April 2020, horror fans reported less stress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Clasen has suggested that horror could work like a "fear vaccine." However, this does not prove that horror makes people stronger, because people who cope well with stress may simply be more likely to enjoy horror.
If you do not like being scared, Kerr suggests watching monster movies, since you know they are not real. You can also leave if it becomes too much.
